questions.q: In the circuit-design workflow modeled in this lesson, what is the first step after being given a target state?
options: Measure the target state to determine its probabilities before choosing any gates
Identify a known recipe that produces a state close to the target, as a starting point
Immediately write out the full n-qubit matrix for the entire circuit
Assume the Chapter 3 Bell-state recipe always works unchanged for any target
questions.explain: The workflow starts by recognizing which known recipe gets you close to the target, then identifying exactly what gap remains — not by jumping straight to a full matrix or assuming one fixed recipe always applies.

questions.q: Why does inserting a Z gate on qubit 1, specifically between the H and the CNOT, target the sign of the |11⟩ term and not the other terms?
options: Z flips the sign only where qubit 1 reads 1, and CNOT only produces the |11⟩ term from cases where qubit 1 is already 1 going in — so the sign Z introduces on qubit 1's |1⟩ component carries through specifically into the |11⟩ output term
Z only acts on qubit 2, so it directly targets whichever term has qubit 2 equal to 1
Z always flips the global sign of the entire state vector, affecting all terms equally
Z has no defined action unless CNOT is applied first
questions.explain: Z's effect is confined to components where the qubit it acts on is |1⟩. Since CNOT turns q1=1 inputs into q2=1 outputs, the sign Z puts on q1's |1⟩ component before CNOT ends up specifically on the resulting |11⟩ term after CNOT.

questions.q: Tracing H, then Z on qubit 1, then CNOT(control=q1,target=q2) starting from |00⟩, what is the verified final state vector in the |00⟩,|01⟩,|10⟩,|11⟩ basis?
questions.explain: Step-by-step: H gives [0.7071,0,0.7071,0]; Z on q1 flips the sign on the |10⟩ component, giving [0.7071,0,-0.7071,0]; CNOT swaps the |10⟩ and |11⟩ amplitudes, giving [0.7071,0,0,-0.7071] — exactly (|00⟩-|11⟩)/√2, matching the specification.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist on numerically verifying the proposed gate sequence rather than trusting the Step 2 reasoning alone?
options: Because Step 2's reasoning about Z was actually wrong and verification was needed to find a completely different gate
Because circuit diagrams cannot be drawn until a numerical state vector has been computed first
Because reasoning about which gate should close a gap can be correct in direction but still needs to be checked term-by-term against the actual amplitudes before it can be trusted as the answer
Because node computations are required by convention even when the answer is already obviously certain
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly notes the Step 2 intuition turned out correct, but the point is that intuition about which gate to try is not the same thing as confirmation — only tracing the actual amplitudes through all three gates confirms the result matches the target exactly.

questions.q: In the finished circuit diagram q1: ──H──Z──●── / q2: ────────X── (vertical line connecting ● and X), in what order are the three gates applied to qubit 1, reading left to right?
options: CNOT first, then H, then Z
H first, then Z, then the control role in CNOT
H and Z simultaneously in one layer, with no CNOT involved on qubit 1 at all
Z first, then H, then CNOT
questions.explain: Reading the q1 wire left to right: the H box comes first, then the Z box, then the control dot of the CNOT — exactly the order H, Z, CNOT used in the verification.
